images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of PAD, which combines scene-level advantages from an independent calibration split with projected planning gradients and local training geometry to estimate the planner-relative influence of each demonstration, enabling budgeted selection of beneficial data for retraining.
Figure 5:Representative NavTest trajectories across policy families. Full-pool synthetic training produces zero-score failures, whereas PAD retains feasible, higher-scoring predictions.

Figure 6:Cross-policy improvements on two representative NavTest scenes.
Within each scene, rows show DiffusionDrive, LTF, and MeanFuser under real-only training (Vanilla, black) and PAD curation (blue).

Figure 7:Representative failures induced by full-pool synthetic training.
Rows show two scenes per policy. Black, orange, and blue denote the real-only, full-pool SimScale, and PAD trajectories, respectively.

Figure 8:Component-wise effects of PAD. Black and blue denote the real-only and PAD trajectories. Metric arrows report the change from real-only training to PAD.
Across policies, PAD improves safety, drivable-area compliance, lane keeping, or progress without degrading the paired component shown in each row.

Figure 9:Representative unresolved failures for DiffusionDrive, LTF, and
MeanFuser. Black and blue denote the real-only and PAD trajectories. Both
variants fail the indicated time-to-collision, traffic-rule, or
drivable-area criterion.
